conversation.content: I give a small nod, then hesitate. "Most days I can still laugh... maybe not as easily as before, but yes, I can still find things to smile at."
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I offer a weak smile. “Good.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I glance down at my hands. “Not really. Even little things I used to like—coffee with a friend or a walk—feel like chores. I still try, but the excitement just isn’t there.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

I press my lips together and nod slowly. “Yeah… more than I’d like to admit. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, my first thought is I must be doing something wrong—like I’m missing some obvious ‘mom instinct’ everyone else has.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I shift in the chair and tuck a strand of hair behind my ear. “Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly wonder if she’s breathing right, or if the rash on her neck is meningitis, or if I sterilised the bottles properly. There doesn’t have to be a trigger—it just floods in.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I clasp my hands tightly in my lap. “Yes… a few times this week. It’s like a rush of heat and my heart starts racing. I’ll be rocking her in the nursery and suddenly feel sure something awful is about to happen, even though everything looks fine. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.”
Things have been getting on top of me

I let out a slow sigh. “Most of the time. Between feedings, laundry, trying to sleep in short bursts—I keep thinking, ‘I can’t keep all these plates spinning.’ I still manage the basics, but it feels like I’m one spilled bottle away from everything crashing.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I rub my eyes. “Yeah. Once she’s finally asleep, my mind just replays every tiny thing I did wrong, and I can’t switch it off. Some nights it takes an hour or two before I drift off, even when I’m exhausted.”
I have felt sad or miserable
“Most days,” I say, voice low. “It’s like this heavy blanket I can’t shake. I’ll see the sun coming through the curtains and think I should feel happy, but instead I just feel… flat and weepy.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I nod quickly, eyes stinging again. “A couple of evenings I just sat on the nursery rug after she finally nodded off and the tears came—quiet, unstoppable. Sometimes it’s a few minutes, sometimes longer, but it’s been more days than not this week.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
I shake my head firmly. “Never. I don’t want to hurt myself—I just want to feel like myself again.”

You've shared that most days feel heavy and joyless, that waves of worry or panic arrive uninvited, and that bedtime brings racing thoughts rather than rest. Despite these struggles, you remain devoted to your baby and hopeful you can feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 21, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>The patient's 'weak smile' and single-word 'Good' indicate a notable reduction in their ability to enjoy humor, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient describes marked loss of anticipatory pleasure—still attempts activities lack previous enjoyment (anhedonia).</sym>, <sym>She describes frequent self-blame tied to perceived maternal instinct deficiency</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily intrusive worries without triggers, matching 'very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden episodes of intense fear with no trigger ('a few times this week… sure something awful is about to happen') that resolve quickly but leave her shaky; frequency and severity match 'Yes, sometimes'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent coping struggles ('most of the time') but retains basic functioning, matching option 2</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most days" and describes persistent low mood with anhedonia and tearfulness, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Matches 'quite often' because tears occurred on more days than not but not most of the time</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 21 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. You describe core symptoms that overlap with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most days, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness, disrupted sleep, and recurrent anxiety attacks. Your self-harm denial on Q10 is reassuring, yet the overall score signals clinically significant distress requiring prompt evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> and therapy options such as <med>CBT</med> or interpersonal therapy
3. Discuss whether <med>antidepressant medication</med> safe for breastfeeding might help
4. Share these EPDS results and your responses with your provider so they can complete a full diagnostic assessment
5. Enlist trusted family or friends to help with night feeds and household tasks so you can obtain 4-5 hours of uninterrupted rest
6. Use brief self-care strategies: 10 minutes of gentle movement, balanced snacks every 3-4 hours, and calming breathing when panic rises
7. Keep crisis resources handy: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US) or local emergency services for any safety concerns
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
